{"@text":"1\nEuropean Industrial Policy:\nThe Airbus Case\nDamien Neven, University of Lausanne\nPaul Seabright, University of Cambridge\n1\n                                                \n \n   \n1\n This paper reports the results of a simulation study commissioned by the UK Department of\nTrade and Industry (EC/4878). Extracts from the Study are reproduced with the permission of\nthe DTI and the Controller of HMSO. We are grateful to the Air Division of DTI, and especially\nto Michael Hodson and Robert Waters, for their detailed help and advice; to John Sutton for\ncomments on the report of the original study; to David Begg and Gene Grossman for comments\non the first draft of this paper; to Lars-Hendrik Roeller for comments and advice throughout the\nproject; and to Lisa Anderson for outstanding research assistance. The usual disclaimer applies\nwith particular force: the views reported in the paper are those of the authors alone, and not\nthose of any of the above individuals or institutions.\n\n2\nAbstract\nThis paper estimates the impact that Airbus’s presence has had on the market for large\ncommercial airliners.  Our model reproduces (in a multi-stage) game a stylised characterisation\nof six main stages in the development of the large commercial airliner market, allowing for\nthree players (Boeing, Airbus and McDonnell Douglas) and four market segments.  The model\nis then used to ask a number of counterfactual questions about what would have happened in a\nvariety of circumstances (notably ones in which Airbus did not enter the market).  Besides\ncapacity and product developments, we also model the level of expenditures on research an\ndevelopment in order to see whether Airbus’s presence has had an impact on the type and\ntechnological specification of aircrafts produced. {"@text":"Review\nAdventures in Semantic Publishing: Exemplar Semantic\nEnhancements of a Research Article\nDavid Shotton*, Katie Portwin, Graham Klyne, Alistair Miles\nImage Bioinformatics Research Group, Department of Zoology, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom\nAbstract:Scientific innovation depends on finding,\nintegrating, and re-using the products of previous\nresearch. Here we explore how recent developments in\nWeb technology, particularly those related to the\npublication of data and metadata, might assist that\nprocess by providing semantic enhancements to journal\narticles within the mainstream process of scholarly journal\npublishing. We exemplify this by describing semantic\nenhancements we have made to a recent biomedical\nresearch article taken fromPLoS Neglected Tropical\nDiseases, providing enrichment to its content and\nincreased access to datasets within it. These semantic\nenhancements include provision of live DOIs and hyper-\nlinks; semantic markup of textual terms, with links to\nrelevant third-party information resources; interactive\nfigures; a re-orderable reference list; a document summary\ncontaining a study summary, a tag cloud, and a citation\nanalysis; and two novel types of semantic enrichment: the\nfirst, a Supporting Claims Tooltip to permit ‘‘Citations in\nContext’’, and the second, Tag Trees that bring together\nsemantically related terms. In addition, we have published\ndownloadable spreadsheets containing data from within\ntables and figures, have enriched these with provenance\ninformation, and have demonstrated various types of data\nfusion (mashups) with results from other research articles\nand with Google Maps. We have also published machine-\nreadable RDF metadata both about the article and about\nthe references it cites, for which we developed a Citation\nTyping Ontology, CiTO (http://purl.org/net/cito/). The\nenhanced article, which is available at http://dx.doi.org/\n10.1371/journal.pntd.0000228.x001, presents a compel-\nling existence proof of the possibilities of semantic\npublication. We hope the showcase of examples and\nideas it contains, described in this paper, will excite the\nimaginations of researchers and publishers, stimulating\nthem to explore the possibilities of semantic publishing\nfor their own research articles, and thereby break down\npresent barriers to the discovery and re-use of information\nwithin traditional modes of scholarly communication.\nIntroduction\nOnline versions of journal articles are conventionally presented\neither as HTML Web pages or as static PDF documents, with the\nWeb used primarily as a convenient distribution medium for\ntraditional text. As the electronic embodiment of the printed page,\nthe PDF document is both familiar and easy for humans to read,\nbut it is antithetical to the spirit of the Web, lacking user\ninteractivity and being difficult for machines to read, thus\ninhibiting the development of services that can automatically link\ninformation between articles.\nRecent developments in Web technology can be used for\nsemantic enhancement of scholarly journals articles, providing\nbetter linking to other resources, adding descriptive metadata that\nassist article discovery and specify the meaning of concepts and\nterms within the article, and allowing users access to ‘‘lively’’\ncontent in the form of interactive figures, re-orderable reference\nlists, document summaries, and downloadable numerical datasets\nin which the data are both accessible and actionable.\nIn this paper we describe semantic enhancements made to a\nrecently published biomedical research article from the journal\nPLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases(PLoS NTDs), using this single\nexemplar research article to create a compelling proof of the\npossibilities of semantic publication.\nWe define the termsemantic publicationto include anything that\nenhances the meaning of a published journal article, facilitates its\nautomated discovery, enables its linking to semantically related\narticles, provides access to data within the article in actionable\nform, or facilitates integration of data between articles.\nWe undertook this exercise in semantic publishing to demon-\nstrate some of the different types of semantic enhancement that we\nconsider desirable for improving the usefulness of online research\narticles, and to show the benefits that ensue from publishing the\ndata they contain to the Web, thus facilitating the integration of\ninformation from different publications.\nThe Unique Role of the Journal Article\nSince our contention is that biomedical journal articles should\nbecome better conduits for the publication of research data than\nthey are at present, it is important to relate them to\nbioinformatics databases, whose primary role is clearly data\npublication. In 2005, Philip E. {"@text":"Towards a Semantic Search Engine\nfor Scientiﬁc Articles\nBastien Latard\n1,2(B)\n, Jonathan Weber\n1\n, Germain Forestier\n1\n,\nand Michel Hassenforder\n1\n1\nMIPS, University of Haute-Alsace, Mulhouse, France\nbastien.latrad@uha.fr\n2\nMDPI AG, Basel, Switzerland\nAbstract.Because of the data deluge in scientiﬁc publication, ﬁnding\nrelevant information is getting harder and harder for researchers and read-\ners. Building an enhanced scientiﬁc search engine by taking semantic rela-\ntions into account poses a great challenge. As a starting point, semantic\nrelations between keywords from scientiﬁc articles could be extracted in\norder to classify articles. This might help later in the process of browsing\nand searching for content in a meaningful scientiﬁc way. Indeed, by con-\nnecting keywords, the context of the article can be extracted. This paper\naims to provide ideas to build such a smart search engine and describes\nthe initial contributions towards achieving such an ambitious goal.\n1 Introduction\nKeeping up-to-date in a speciﬁc research ﬁeld is a tedious and complex task. This\nis mandatory as it allows researchers to increase their knowledge on a domain and\nacquire latest ideas. Hence, choosing the correct approach is the ﬁrst step of any\nresearch work. Despite—or because of—the data deluge in scientiﬁc publication,\nresearchers spend a signiﬁcant amount of time searching for articles related to\ntheir scientiﬁc interests.\nAn editorial fromNature[1] clearly expressed the continued frustration of\nthe scientiﬁc community concerning the incredible potential that text mining\nof scientiﬁc literature represents. However, text miners often face the barrier of\npublishers’ legal restrictions (i.e., closed access). The average growth of scien-\ntiﬁc literature is estimated to be 3 million new articles per year from journals\nand conferences over the last 4 years, with 3.3 million articles produced in 2016\n(http://www.scilit.net). This massive amount of data is published by more than\n6000 publishers in around 47,000 scientiﬁc journals. These de-centralised and\nseparated platforms further complicate the research process because scientists\nare unable to go through them all in order to search for relevant articles. Thus,\nthey have to rely on big databases or indexing companies which provide either\nan incomplete corpus due to selection criteria or only display articles from their\nown platforms. Moreover, their search engines often oﬀer very limited search\nfunctionalities, and this is the problem we want to tackle.\ncﬀSpringer International Publishing AG 2017\nJ. Kamps et al. (Eds.): TPDL 2017, LNCS 10450, pp. 608–611, 2017.\nDOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-67008-9\n54\n\nTowards a Semantic Search Engine for Scientiﬁc Articles 609\nTo tackle this problem, our approach consists in using semantic relations\nbetween keywords to extract the main categories of the articles. This approach\nsimultaneously validates both the context of the article and the context of the\nword, thus providing the correct category. Eﬀendy and Yap [2] discussed the\npotential of using semantic mining tools to extract the best category of a con-\nference. This is exactly what our framework aims to do.\n2Method\nOur approach uses BabelNet [3] which is a multilingual lexicographic and ency-\nclopaedic database based on the smart superposition of semantic lexicons (Word-\nNet, VerbNet) together with other collaborative databases (Wikipedia and other\nWiki data). A query for a term through BabelNet returns “dictionary entries”,\nsynonyms, categories or domains. Each synsetScontains the relative categories\nC, domainsDand synonymssynwithin the speciﬁc concept:\nS\u003d{C, D, syn}\t(1)\nAssuming that synonyms of keywords might be an interesting way to connect\nseveral articles, BabelNet is the knowledge database on which our framework will\nrely. However, BabelNet lacks speciﬁcity and searching for one word can return\nsynsets from various diﬀerent contexts. For example, “ﬂight” returns 36 synsets,\nfrom a South Korean movie to the verb ‘to ﬂy’. Consequently, a method to ﬁlter\nout unrelated synsets is mandatory.\nBecause synonyms are too speciﬁc, and domains are too general, categories\nhave been naturally chosen in order to identify overlapping between synsets from\ndiﬀerent keywords. Indeed, if several keywords share the same category, then this\nis potentially the correct category in regards to the article context. In addition,\nthe greater the number of keywords sharing the same category, the higher the\nconﬁdence. Thus, connecting the returned synsets based on their categories is\nan interesting way to naturally ﬁlter out all of the unrelated synsets.\nThis approach does ﬁlter some content, but still returns “living people;\nEnglish-language ﬁlms; celestial mechanics; American ﬁlms” as the main cat-\negories for keywords “nonlocal gravity; celestial mechanics; dark matter”. {"@text":"Review\nAdventures in Semantic Publishing: Exemplar Semantic\nEnhancements of a Research Article\nDavid Shotton*, Katie Portwin, Graham Klyne, Alistair Miles\nImage Bioinformatics Research Group, Department of Zoology, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom\nAbstract:Scientific innovation depends on finding,\nintegrating, and re-using the products of previous\nresearch. Here we explore how recent developments in\nWeb technology, particularly those related to the\npublication of data and metadata, might assist that\nprocess by providing semantic enhancements to journal\narticles within the mainstream process of scholarly journal\npublishing. We exemplify this by describing semantic\nenhancements we have made to a recent biomedical\nresearch article taken fromPLoS Neglected Tropical\nDiseases, providing enrichment to its content and\nincreased access to datasets within it. These semantic\nenhancements include provision of live DOIs and hyper-\nlinks; semantic markup of textual terms, with links to\nrelevant third-party information resources; interactive\nfigures; a re-orderable reference list; a document summary\ncontaining a study summary, a tag cloud, and a citation\nanalysis; and two novel types of semantic enrichment: the\nfirst, a Supporting Claims Tooltip to permit ‘‘Citations in\nContext’’, and the second, Tag Trees that bring together\nsemantically related terms. In addition, we have published\ndownloadable spreadsheets containing data from within\ntables and figures, have enriched these with provenance\ninformation, and have demonstrated various types of data\nfusion (mashups) with results from other research articles\nand with Google Maps. We have also published machine-\nreadable RDF metadata both about the article and about\nthe references it cites, for which we developed a Citation\nTyping Ontology, CiTO (http://purl.org/net/cito/). The\nenhanced article, which is available at http://dx.doi.org/\n10.1371/journal.pntd.0000228.x001, presents a compel-\nling existence proof of the possibilities of semantic\npublication. We hope the showcase of examples and\nideas it contains, described in this paper, will excite the\nimaginations of researchers and publishers, stimulating\nthem to explore the possibilities of semantic publishing\nfor their own research articles, and thereby break down\npresent barriers to the discovery and re-use of information\nwithin traditional modes of scholarly communication.\nIntroduction\nOnline versions of journal articles are conventionally presented\neither as HTML Web pages or as static PDF documents, with the\nWeb used primarily as a convenient distribution medium for\ntraditional text. As the electronic embodiment of the printed page,\nthe PDF document is both familiar and easy for humans to read,\nbut it is antithetical to the spirit of the Web, lacking user\ninteractivity and being difficult for machines to read, thus\ninhibiting the development of services that can automatically link\ninformation between articles.\nRecent developments in Web technology can be used for\nsemantic enhancement of scholarly journals articles, providing\nbetter linking to other resources, adding descriptive metadata that\nassist article discovery and specify the meaning of concepts and\nterms within the article, and allowing users access to ‘‘lively’’\ncontent in the form of interactive figures, re-orderable reference\nlists, document summaries, and downloadable numerical datasets\nin which the data are both accessible and actionable.\nIn this paper we describe semantic enhancements made to a\nrecently published biomedical research article from the journal\nPLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases(PLoS NTDs), using this single\nexemplar research article to create a compelling proof of the\npossibilities of semantic publication.\nWe define the termsemantic publicationto include anything that\nenhances the meaning of a published journal article, facilitates its\nautomated discovery, enables its linking to semantically related\narticles, provides access to data within the article in actionable\nform, or facilitates integration of data between articles.\nWe undertook this exercise in semantic publishing to demon-\nstrate some of the different types of semantic enhancement that we\nconsider desirable for improving the usefulness of online research\narticles, and to show the benefits that ensue from publishing the\ndata they contain to the Web, thus {"@text":"Data and text mining\nThalia: semantic search engine for biomedical\nabstracts\nAxel J. Soto\n, Piotr Przybyła, and Sophia Ananiadou*\nNational Centre for Text Mining, School of Computer Science, University of Manchester, Manchester M1 7DN, UK\n*To whom correspondence should be addressed.\nAssociate Editor: Jonathan Wren\nReceived on June 15, 2018; revised on September 18, 2018; editorial decision on October 5, 2018; accepted on October 16, 2018\nAbstract\nSummary:Although the publication rate of the biomedical literature has been growing steadily\nduring the last decades, the accessibility of pertinent research publications for biologist and medic-\nal practitioners remains a challenge. This article describes Thalia, which is a semantic search en-\ngine that can recognize eight different types of concepts occurring in biomedical abstracts. Thalia\nis available via a web-based interface or a RESTful API. A key aspect of our search engine is that it\nis updated from PubMed on a daily basis. We describe here the main building blocks of our tool as\nwell as an evaluation of the retrieval capabilities of Thalia in the context of a precision medicine\ndataset.\nAvailability and implementation:Thalia is available at http://nactem.ac.uk/Thalia_BI/.\nContact:sophia.ananiadou@manchester.ac.uk\nSupplementary information:Supplementary dataare available atBioinformaticsonline.\nThe volume, variety and rate of publication for the biomedical scien-\ntific literature make it an exemplary case of Big Data and of its in-\nherent challenges. In this information overload scenario, the\naccurate retrieval of relevant information from such a large volume\nof written knowledge becomes a necessary asset for biologists and\nmedical practitioners alike (Gonzalezet al., 2016).\nIn this article, we present Thalia—Text mining for Highlighting,\nAggregating and Linking Information in Articles—which is a seman-\ntic search tool for the biomedical literature. Its semantic capacity\noriginates from the automatic mining of concepts occurring in\narticles indexed in PubMed (NCBI Resource Coordinators, 2017)\nand its normalization to specialized ontologies. In this way, it is pos-\nsible to search and retrieve all documents containing any mentions\nof a given concept regardless of the textual variation that is used to\nrepresent that concept. Similarly, polysemy—i.e. a same term having\nmultiple meanings—is resolved based on the context where a term\noccurs. Thalia currently recognizes eight types of concepts, namely:\nchemicals, diseases, drugs, genes, metabolites, proteins, species and\nanatomical entities.\nAlthough similar search systems have been made available before\n(Hoehndorfet al., 2015;Leeet al., 2016;Lu, 2011;Mu¨ lleret al.,\n2017;Thomaset al., 2012;Weiet al., 2013), there are several dis-\ntinctive aspects of Thalia:\n1. It is updated daily by automatically downloading updates from\nPubMed, mining concepts and adding them to the search index.\nThis is a crucial feature, as systems lacking it quickly become\noutdated after deployment.\n2. Thalia’s named entity recognition (NER) methods have been\ncustomized for biomedical entity mining as a result of years of\nresearch and participation in shared tasks.\n3. Thalia uses a context-sensitive acronym resolution in order to\nimprove concept recognition.\n4. It provides a visual interface, which allows autocompletion and\nconcept aggregation, as well as a RESTful API that enables pro-\ngrammatic access to the search system.\nTo recognize named entities from the literature, Thalia uses com-\nponents of Argo (Raket al., 2012), which is a text mining workflow\nsystem. This includes NER modules for chemicals, drugs and metab-\nolites (Kolluruet al., 2011;Nobataet al., 2011), genes, diseases and\nproteins (Raket al., 2014), species (Wanget al., 2010), and anatom-\nical entities (Pyysalo and Ananiadou, 2014). Airbus was the first manufacturer to install an electric flight \ncontrol system on the A320. In 2013, Airbus produced 626 aircraft and won \n1,503 net orders. Airbus was the first manufacturer to install an electric flight \ncontrol system on the A320. In 2013, Airbus produced 626 aircraft and won \n1,503 net orders. Airbus was the first manufacturer to install an electric flight \ncontrol system on the A320. In 2013, Airbus produced 626 aircraft and won \n1,503 net orders. {"@text":"1\nEuropean Industrial Policy:\nThe Airbus Case\nDamien Neven, University of Lausanne\nPaul Seabright, University of Cambridge\n1\n                                                \n \n   \n1\n This paper reports the results of a simulation study commissioned by the UK Department of\nTrade and Industry (EC/4878). Extracts from the Study are reproduced with the permission of\nthe DTI and the Controller of HMSO. We are grateful to the Air Division of DTI, and especially\nto Michael Hodson and Robert Waters, for their detailed help and advice; to John Sutton for\ncomments on the report of the original study; to David Begg and Gene Grossman for comments\non the first draft of this paper; to Lars-Hendrik Roeller for comments and advice throughout the\nproject; and to Lisa Anderson for outstanding research assistance. The usual disclaimer applies\nwith particular force: the views reported in the paper are those of the authors alone, and not\nthose of any of the above individuals or institutions.\n\n2\nAbstract\nThis paper estimates the impact that Airbus’s presence has had on the market for large\ncommercial airliners.  Our model reproduces (in a multi-stage) game a stylised characterisation\nof six main stages in the development of the large commercial airliner market, allowing for\nthree players (Boeing, Airbus and McDonnell Douglas) and four market segments.  The model\nis then used to ask a number of counterfactual questions about what would have happened in a\nvariety of circumstances (notably ones in which Airbus did not enter the market).  Besides\ncapacity and product developments, we also model the level of expenditures on research an\ndevelopment in order to see whether Airbus’s presence has had an impact on the type and\ntechnological specification of aircrafts produced.  We find that given the prior presence of\nMcDonnell Douglas in this market, Airbus has had only a modest impact on the prices of\ncommercial airlines (an average of 3.5%).  The reasons are twofold : first, although the Airbus\npresence constraints the actions of Boeing, it weakens the incentive for McDonnell Douglas to\ncompete vigorously with Boeing.  Secondly, by reducing Boeing’s market share, it prevents the\nrealisation of the substantial economies of scale and scope that are believed to exist in this\ntechnology.  Overall, this means that the consumer surplus argument for government subsidy to\nAirbus is only weakly supported by the model.  Consumer surplus benefits from a challenge to\nBoeing have certainly been substantial but most of them could have been achieved by\nMcDonnell Douglas on its own.  In terms of product development, we find that although\nAirbus may have deterred McDonnell Douglas from producing an aircraft in the same category\nof the A 300 (medium range, medium-bodied), it may in contrast have actually made it easier\n\n3\nfor McDonnell Douglas to produce the MD-11 in competition with the A 330/340 and the\nBoeing 777.  This is because the loss of scale and scope economies by Boeing as a result of the\nAirbus entry has substantially raised the cost to Boeing of producing the 777, making entry\nmore attractive for McDonnell Douglas even when Airbus’s presence is taken into account. \nFinally, we find that the presence of Airbus reduces Boeing’s profits by at least $ 100 bn and\nMcDonnell Douglas’s by two-thirds.  Airbus itself makes profits which are difficult to estimate\nwith confidence, but which may lie somewhere between $49bn and $52bn, of the order of a\nbillion dollars per annum and equivalent to a rate of return over the whole period of between\n6% and 11%.   If we give the same weight to profits and consumer surplus, this implies that\nAirbus has had a large negative impact on world welfare but a comfortably positive impact on\nEuropean welfare.\n\n4\n  \n1. Introduction\nWhen should governments intervene to promote specific types of productive activity in\nthe economy? Answers to this question have been subject to periodic swings of fashion, but a\nconsensus has gradually emerged that intervention needs to be based on a sound account of\nwhy unaided markets will fail to encourage adequately efficient levels of the activities\nconcerned, as well as a reasonable optimism that government failures will not lead to\ndistortions as significant as those market failures it is sought to correct. The application of this\nconsensus to actual cases, however, has generated substantial discord, particularly when the\nactivities under discussion are not public goods, but private goods which for one reason or\nanother are claimed to be supplied in inadequate quantity or quality. That the state should be a\nvigilant referee of the competitive process is a view that would command widespread assent;\nthat it should be an active player in the competitive game is a much more debated and\ndebatable claim.\nIn no specific field of economic activity has the debate been more vigorous than in\ncommercial aerospace, where production has been supported and encouraged in covert {"@text":"Review\nAdventures in Semantic Publishing: Exemplar Semantic\nEnhancements of a Research Article\nDavid Shotton*, Katie Portwin, Graham Klyne, Alistair Miles\nImage Bioinformatics Research Group, Department of Zoology, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom\nAbstract:Scientific innovation depends on finding,\nintegrating, and re-using the products of previous\nresearch. Here we explore how recent developments in\nWeb technology, particularly those related to the\npublication of data and metadata, might assist that\nprocess by providing semantic enhancements to journal\narticles within the mainstream process of scholarly journal\npublishing. We exemplify this by describing semantic\nenhancements we have made to a recent biomedical\nresearch article taken fromPLoS Neglected Tropical\nDiseases, providing enrichment to its content and\nincreased access to datasets within it. These semantic\nenhancements include provision of live DOIs and hyper-\nlinks; semantic markup of textual terms, with links to\nrelevant third-party information resources; interactive\nfigures; a re-orderable reference list; a document summary\ncontaining a study summary, a tag cloud, and a citation\nanalysis; and two novel types of semantic enrichment: the\nfirst, a Supporting Claims Tooltip to permit ‘‘Citations in\nContext’’, and the second, Tag Trees that bring together\nsemantically related terms. In addition, we have published\ndownloadable spreadsheets containing data from within\ntables and figures, have enriched these with provenance\ninformation, and have demonstrated various types of data\nfusion (mashups) with results from other research articles\nand with Google Maps. We have also published machine-\nreadable RDF metadata both about the article and about\nthe references it cites, for which we developed a Citation\nTyping Ontology, CiTO (http://purl.org/net/cito/). The\nenhanced article, which is available at http://dx.doi.org/\n10.1371/journal.pntd.0000228.x001, presents a compel-\nling existence proof of the possibilities of semantic\npublication. We hope the showcase of examples and\nideas it contains, described in this paper, will excite the\nimaginations of researchers and publishers, stimulating\nthem to explore the possibilities of semantic publishing\nfor their own research articles, and thereby break down\npresent barriers to the discovery and re-use of information\nwithin traditional modes of scholarly communication.\nIntroduction\nOnline versions of journal articles are conventionally presented\neither as HTML Web pages or as static PDF documents, with the\nWeb used primarily as a convenient distribution medium for\ntraditional text. As the electronic embodiment of the printed page,\nthe PDF document is both familiar and easy for humans to read,\nbut it is antithetical to the spirit of the Web, lacking user\ninteractivity and being difficult for machines to read, thus\ninhibiting the development of services that can automatically link\ninformation between articles.\nRecent developments in Web technology can be used for\nsemantic enhancement of scholarly journals articles, providing\nbetter linking to other resources, adding descriptive metadata that\nassist article discovery and specify the meaning of concepts and\nterms within the article, and allowing users access to ‘‘lively’’\ncontent in the form of interactive figures, re-orderable reference\nlists, document summaries, and downloadable numerical datasets\nin which the data are both accessible and actionable.\nIn this paper we describe semantic enhancements made to a\nrecently published biomedical research article from the journal\nPLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases(PLoS NTDs), using this single\nexemplar research article to create a compelling proof of the\npossibilities of semantic publication.\nWe define the termsemantic publicationto include anything that\nenhances the meaning of a published journal article, facilitates its\nautomated discovery, enables its linking to semantically related\narticles, provides access to data within the article in actionable\nform, or facilitates integration of data between articles.\nWe undertook this exercise in semantic publishing to demon-\nstrate some of the different types of semantic enhancement that we\nconsider desirable for improving the usefulness of online research\narticles, and to show the benefits that ensue from publishing the\ndata they contain to the Web, thus facilitating the integration of\ninformation from different publications.\nThe Unique Role of the Journal Article\nSince our contention is that biomedical journal articles should\nbecome better conduits for the publication of research data than\nthey are at present, it is important to relate them to\nbioinformatics databases, whose primary role is clearly data\npublication. In 2005, Philip E. Bourne, Editor-in Chief ofPLoS\nComputational Biologyand Co-Director of the Protein Data Bank\n(PDB; http://www.rcsb.org/pdb/), wrote a stimulating article [1]\nin which he pointed out that the distinction between an online\npaper and a database was diminishing and called for ‘‘seamless\nintegration’’ between papers reporting results and the datasets\nused to compute those results.\nCitation:Shotton D, Portwin K, Klyne G, Miles A (2009) Adventures in Semantic\nPublishing: Exemplar Semantic Enhancements of a Research Article. PLoS Comput\nBiol 5(4): e1000361. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000361\nEditor:Philip E. Bourne, University of California San Diego, United States of\nAmerica\nCopyright:\u00012009 Shotton et al. This is an open-access article distributed\nunder the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits\nunrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the\noriginal author and source are credited.\nFunding:The authors received no specific funding for this article.\nCompeting Interests:David Shotton is a judge for the Elsevier Grand\nChallenge, but the enhancements for this paper were conceived and executed\nindependently from that competition and in advance of his access to\ncompetitors’ EGC entries. The other authors of the enhancements have declared\nthat no competing interests exist.\n* E-mail: david.shotton@zoo.ox.ac.uk\nPublishedApril 17, 2009\nPLoS Computational Biology | www.ploscompbiol.org 1 April 2009 | Volume 5 | Issue 4 | e1000361\n\nWhile we agree with his central analysis that in the electronic\nage the processes involved in submitting papers to journals and\ndata to bioinformatics databases are essentially similar, we contend\nthat similarity of process should not blind us to essential differences\nin purpose. Anita de Waard [2] has argued persuasively that the\nscientific journal article is an exercise in rhetoric, with the primary\npurpose of persuading readers of the truth of a particular\nhypothesis, and that the data it contains are carefully selected to\nprove that hypothesis as clearly as possible. {"@text":"Towards a Semantic Search Engine\nfor Scientiﬁc Articles\nBastien Latard\n1,2(B)\n, Jonathan Weber\n1\n, Germain Forestier\n1\n,\nand Michel Hassenforder\n1\n1\nMIPS, University of Haute-Alsace, Mulhouse, France\nbastien.latrad@uha.fr\n2\nMDPI AG, Basel, Switzerland\nAbstract.Because of the data deluge in scientiﬁc publication, ﬁnding\nrelevant information is getting harder and harder for researchers and read-\ners. Building an enhanced scientiﬁc search engine by taking semantic rela-\ntions into account poses a great challenge. As a starting point, semantic\nrelations between keywords from scientiﬁc articles could be extracted in\norder to classify articles. This might help later in the process of browsing\nand searching for content in a meaningful scientiﬁc way. Indeed, by con-\nnecting keywords, the context of the article can be extracted. This paper\naims to provide ideas to build such a smart search engine and describes\nthe initial contributions towards achieving such an ambitious goal.\n1 Introduction\nKeeping up-to-date in a speciﬁc research ﬁeld is a tedious and complex task. This\nis mandatory as it allows researchers to increase their knowledge on a domain and\nacquire latest ideas. Hence, choosing the correct approach is the ﬁrst step of any\nresearch work. Despite—or because of—the data deluge in scientiﬁc publication,\nresearchers spend a signiﬁcant amount of time searching for articles related to\ntheir scientiﬁc interests.\nAn editorial fromNature[1] clearly expressed the continued frustration of\nthe scientiﬁc community concerning the incredible potential that text mining\nof scientiﬁc literature represents. However, text miners often face the barrier of\npublishers’ legal restrictions (i.e., closed access). The average growth of scien-\ntiﬁc literature is estimated to be 3 million new articles per year from journals\nand conferences over the last 4 years, with 3.3 million articles produced in 2016\n(http://www.scilit.net). This massive amount of data is published by more than\n6000 publishers in around 47,000 scientiﬁc journals. These de-centralised and\nseparated platforms further complicate the research process because scientists\nare unable to go through them all in order to search for relevant articles. Thus,\nthey have to rely on big databases or indexing companies which provide either\nan incomplete corpus due to selection criteria or only display articles from their\nown platforms. Moreover, their search engines often oﬀer very limited search\nfunctionalities, and this is the problem we want to tackle.\ncﬀSpringer International Publishing AG 2017\nJ. Kamps et al. (Eds.): TPDL 2017, LNCS 10450, pp. 608–611, 2017.\nDOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-67008-9\n54\n\nTowards a Semantic Search Engine for Scientiﬁc Articles 609\nTo tackle this problem, our approach consists in using semantic relations\nbetween keywords to extract the main categories of the articles. This approach\nsimultaneously validates both the context of the article and the context of the\nword, thus providing the correct category. Eﬀendy and Yap [2] discussed the\npotential of using semantic mining tools to extract the best category of a con-\nference. This is exactly what our framework aims to do.\n2Method\nOur approach uses BabelNet [3] which is a multilingual lexicographic and ency-\nclopaedic database based on the smart superposition of semantic lexicons (Word-\nNet, VerbNet) together with other collaborative databases (Wikipedia and other\nWiki data). A query for a term through BabelNet returns “dictionary entries”,\nsynonyms, categories or domains. Each synsetScontains the relative categories\nC, domainsDand synonymssynwithin the speciﬁc concept:\nS\u003d{C, D, syn}\t(1)\nAssuming that synonyms of keywords might be an interesting way to connect\nseveral articles, BabelNet is the knowledge database on which our framework will\nrely. However, BabelNet lacks speciﬁcity and searching for one word can return\nsynsets from various diﬀerent contexts. For example, “ﬂight” returns 36 synsets,\nfrom a South Korean movie to the verb ‘to ﬂy’. Consequently, a method to ﬁlter\nout unrelated synsets is mandatory.\nBecause synonyms are too speciﬁc, and domains are too general, categories\nhave been naturally chosen in order to identify overlapping between synsets from\ndiﬀerent keywords. Indeed, if several keywords share the same category, then this\nis potentially the correct category in regards to the article context. In addition,\nthe greater the number of keywords sharing the same category, the higher the\nconﬁdence. Thus, connecting the returned synsets based on their categories is\nan interesting way to naturally ﬁlter out all of the unrelated synsets.\nThis approach does ﬁlter some content, but still returns “living people;\nEnglish-language ﬁlms; celestial mechanics; American ﬁlms” as the main cat-\negories for keywords “nonlocal gravity; celestial mechanics; dark matter”. Con-\nstant noise (*\nsinger,*album, etc.), meaningless in our scientiﬁc context, has\nbeen identiﬁed. A parameter can now be set in order to force the automatic ﬁl-\ntering of identiﬁed noise. Most of the remaining noise is ﬁnally naturally ﬁltered\nout, and “celestial mechanics” is ﬁnally returned as the main category.\nOur ﬁnal goal is to apply this valuable added knowledge to all articles from\nthe scientiﬁc literature database, Scilit (http://www.scilit.net), developed by\nMDPI (http://www.mdpi.com). To validate our approach, a manual analysis\non a subset of 595 articles from seven journals (six about Physical Science and\none about Pediatrics) has been conducted. We evaluated the correctness of the\ncategories based on the connection of keywords by their synsets. This approach\nprovides good precision—from 96% to 100%—depending on the threshold which\nidentify the data as correct not. Indeed, strictly selecting only categories shared\n\n610 B. Latard et al.\nby three diﬀerent keywords or more leads to a high degree of conﬁdence (100%\nprecision), but a recall of 9%. By being more tolerant and considering all cate-\ngories shared by at least two keywords, precision slightly decreased (96%) but\nwe signiﬁcantly gain in recall (47%). Moreover, similar proportions are observed\nforChildren, the journal about Pediatrics (from 100% to 92%). This validates\nthat our approach may be used in several domains.\nThe main drawback of our approach is that correct categories have been\nidentiﬁed for only 22% of the articles within the subset. {"@text":"Review\nAdventures in Semantic Publishing: Exemplar Semantic\nEnhancements of a Research Article\nDavid Shotton*, Katie Portwin, Graham Klyne, Alistair Miles\nImage Bioinformatics Research Group, Department of Zoology, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom\nAbstract:Scientific innovation depends on finding,\nintegrating, and re-using the products of previous\nresearch. Here we explore how recent developments in\nWeb technology, particularly those related to the\npublication of data and metadata, might assist that\nprocess by providing semantic enhancements to journal\narticles within the mainstream process of scholarly journal\npublishing. We exemplify this by describing semantic\nenhancements we have made to a recent biomedical\nresearch article taken fromPLoS Neglected Tropical\nDiseases, providing enrichment to its content and\nincreased access to datasets within it. These semantic\nenhancements include provision of live DOIs and hyper-\nlinks; semantic markup of textual terms, with links to\nrelevant third-party information resources; interactive\nfigures; a re-orderable reference list; a document summary\ncontaining a study summary, a tag cloud, and a citation\nanalysis; and two novel types of semantic enrichment: the\nfirst, a Supporting Claims Tooltip to permit ‘‘Citations in\nContext’’, and the second, Tag Trees that bring together\nsemantically related terms. In addition, we have published\ndownloadable spreadsheets containing data from within\ntables and figures, have enriched these with provenance\ninformation, and have demonstrated various types of data\nfusion (mashups) with results from other research articles\nand with Google Maps. We have also published machine-\nreadable RDF metadata both about the article and about\nthe references it cites, for which we developed a Citation\nTyping Ontology, CiTO (http://purl.org/net/cito/). The\nenhanced article, which is available at http://dx.doi.org/\n10.1371/journal.pntd.0000228.x001, presents a compel-\nling existence proof of the possibilities of semantic\npublication. We hope the showcase of examples and\nideas it contains, described in this paper, will excite the\nimaginations of researchers and publishers, stimulating\nthem to explore the possibilities of semantic publishing\nfor their own research articles, and thereby break down\npresent barriers to the discovery and re-use of information\nwithin traditional modes of scholarly communication.\nIntroduction\nOnline versions of journal articles are conventionally presented\neither as HTML Web pages or as static PDF documents, with the\nWeb used primarily as a convenient distribution medium for\ntraditional text. As the electronic embodiment of the printed page,\nthe PDF document is both familiar and easy for humans to read,\nbut it is antithetical to the spirit of the Web, lacking user\ninteractivity and being difficult for machines to read, thus\ninhibiting the development of services that can automatically link\ninformation between articles.\nRecent developments in Web technology can be used for\nsemantic enhancement of scholarly journals articles, providing\nbetter linking to other resources, adding descriptive metadata that\nassist article discovery and specify the meaning of concepts and\nterms within the article, and allowing users access to ‘‘lively’’\ncontent in the form of interactive figures, re-orderable reference\nlists, document summaries, and downloadable numerical datasets\nin which the data are both accessible and actionable.\nIn this paper we describe semantic enhancements made to a\nrecently published biomedical research article from the journal\nPLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases(PLoS NTDs), using this single\nexemplar research article to create a compelling proof of the\npossibilities of semantic publication.\nWe define the termsemantic publicationto include anything that\nenhances the meaning of a published journal article, facilitates its\nautomated discovery, enables its linking to semantically related\narticles, provides access to data within the article in actionable\nform, or facilitates integration of data between articles.\nWe undertook this exercise in semantic publishing to demon-\nstrate some of the different types of semantic enhancement that we\nconsider desirable for improving the usefulness of online research\narticles, and to show the benefits that ensue from publishing the\ndata they contain to the Web, thus facilitating the integration of\ninformation from different publications.\nThe Unique Role of the Journal Article\nSince our contention is that biomedical journal articles should\nbecome better conduits for the publication of research data than\nthey are at present, it is important to relate them to\nbioinformatics databases, whose primary role is clearly data\npublication. In 2005, Philip E. Bourne, Editor-in Chief ofPLoS\nComputational Biologyand Co-Director of the Protein Data Bank\n(PDB; http://www.rcsb.org/pdb/), wrote a stimulating article [1]\nin which he pointed out that the distinction between an online\npaper and a database was diminishing and called for ‘‘seamless\nintegration’’ between papers reporting results and the datasets\nused to compute those results.\nCitation:Shotton D, Portwin K, Klyne G, Miles A (2009) Adventures in Semantic\nPublishing: Exemplar Semantic Enhancements of a Research Article. In contrast, the\nfunction of a bioinformatics database is to provide impartial access\nto complete datasets. {"@text":"Data and text mining\nThalia: semantic search engine for biomedical\nabstracts\nAxel J. Soto\n, Piotr Przybyła, and Sophia Ananiadou*\nNational Centre for Text Mining, School of Computer Science, University of Manchester, Manchester M1 7DN, UK\n*To whom correspondence should be addressed.\nAssociate Editor: Jonathan Wren\nReceived on June 15, 2018; revised on September 18, 2018; editorial decision on October 5, 2018; accepted on October 16, 2018\nAbstract\nSummary:Although the publication rate of the biomedical literature has been growing steadily\nduring the last decades, the accessibility of pertinent research publications for biologist and medic-\nal practitioners remains a challenge. This article describes Thalia, which is a semantic search en-\ngine that can recognize eight different types of concepts occurring in biomedical abstracts. Thalia\nis available via a web-based interface or a RESTful API. A key aspect of our search engine is that it\nis updated from PubMed on a daily basis. We describe here the main building blocks of our tool as\nwell as an evaluation of the retrieval capabilities of Thalia in the context of a precision medicine\ndataset.\nAvailability and implementation:Thalia is available at http://nactem.ac.uk/Thalia_BI/.\nContact:sophia.ananiadou@manchester.ac.uk\nSupplementary information:Supplementary dataare available atBioinformaticsonline.\nThe volume, variety and rate of publication for the biomedical scien-\ntific literature make it an exemplary case of Big Data and of its in-\nherent challenges. In this information overload scenario, the\naccurate retrieval of relevant information from such a large volume\nof written knowledge becomes a necessary asset for biologists and\nmedical practitioners alike (Gonzalezet al., 2016).\nIn this article, we present Thalia—Text mining for Highlighting,\nAggregating and Linking Information in Articles—which is a seman-\ntic search tool for the biomedical literature. Its semantic capacity\noriginates from the automatic mining of concepts occurring in\narticles indexed in PubMed (NCBI Resource Coordinators, 2017)\nand its normalization to specialized ontologies. In this way, it is pos-\nsible to search and retrieve all documents containing any mentions\nof a given concept regardless of the textual variation that is used to\nrepresent that concept. Similarly, polysemy—i.e. a same term having\nmultiple meanings—is resolved based on the context where a term\noccurs. Thalia currently recognizes eight types of concepts, namely:\nchemicals, diseases, drugs, genes, metabolites, proteins, species and\nanatomical entities.\nAlthough similar search systems have been made available before\n(Hoehndorfet al., 2015;Leeet al., 2016;Lu, 2011;Mu¨ lleret al.,\n2017;Thomaset al., 2012;Weiet al., 2013), there are several dis-\ntinctive aspects of Thalia:\n1. It is updated daily by automatically downloading updates from\nPubMed, mining concepts and adding them to the search index.\nThis is a crucial feature, as systems lacking it quickly become\noutdated after deployment.\n2. Thalia’s named entity recognition (NER) methods have been\ncustomized for biomedical entity mining as a result of years of\nresearch and participation in shared tasks.\n3. Thalia uses a context-sensitive acronym resolution in order to\nimprove concept recognition.\n4. It provides a visual interface, which allows autocompletion and\nconcept aggregation, as well as a RESTful API that enables pro-\ngrammatic access to the search system.\nTo recognize named entities from the literature, Thalia uses com-\nponents of Argo (Raket al., 2012), which is a text mining workflow\nsystem. This includes NER modules for chemicals, drugs and metab-\nolites (Kolluruet al., 2011;Nobataet al., 2011), genes, diseases and\nproteins (Raket al., 2014), species (Wanget al., 2010), and anatom-\nical entities (Pyysalo and Ananiadou, 2014). These models are based\nVCThe Author(s) 2018. Published by Oxford University Press.\t1799\nThis is an Open Access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), which permits unrestricted\nreuse, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited.\nBioinformatics, 35(10), 2019, 1799–1801\ndoi: 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty871\nAdvance Access Publication Date: 17 October 2018\nApplications Note\nDownloaded from https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/35/10/1799/5134063 by University of the Aegean user on 08 November 2023\n\non dictionary matching as well as conditional random fields models\ntrained using human-annotated data. The recognition step is followed\nby a normalization (Batista-Navarroet al.,2016) to concepts from\nthe following ontologies: ChEBI (chemicals), DrugBank (drugs),\nHMDB (metabolites), HGNC (genes), UMLS Metathesaurus (dis-\neases), UniProt (proteins), NCBI (species) and CARO (anatomical).\nWe leverage our acronym disambiguation module (Okazaki\net al., 2010) to improve NER precision and recall. If the long (i.e.\nspelled out) version of an acronym is recognized as a concept by the\nNER, but its short form is not, then we can extend the concept on\nthe short form, too. Similarly, if a concept is recognized in an abbre-\nviated form by the NER, but not as the same concept as the one rec-\nognized in the long form, then we correct the concept recognition in\nthe short form. This follows the observation that long forms are less\nambiguous as NER models can be deceived byad hocabbreviations.\nThe search system was implemented using Elasticsearch (https://\nwww.elastic.co/products/elasticsearch), which can be accessed from a\nweb-based interface written in Javascript (Fig. 1). Semantic search is\nenabled by expanding the query area or by interacting with the differ-\nent entity facets, which suggest the most frequent entities to narrow\ndown the list of retrieved documents. Thalia also allows inspecting\nthe full text of each abstract with its occurring entities highlighted as\nwell as linking to the concepts in the ontology. Alternatively, the API\nallows by passing the visual interface to interact with Thalia’s search\nengine programmatically. The Supplementary Material contains\ndocumentation for the web-based interface and the API, as well as a\nvideo that shows how users can benefit from the semantic search cap-\nacity of Thalia.\nWe evaluated the search capacity of Thalia in a precision medi-\ncine (PM) scenario. In PM, a problem that medical practitioners\nneed to overcome is to find the best treatment given a patient’s\ndisease and her genetic features. Herein, we make use of TREC\n2017 PM shared task data (Robertset al., 2017). The challenge\ninvolved a set of patient cases, which are described by the patient\ndisease, her genetic variance and other demographic information.\nThe goal was to find documents (PubMed entries, conference\nabstracts and clinical trials) that are relevant, i.e. they relate to a po-\ntential treatment for the patient. In \nEurope, the infrastructures of the aeronautical industry \nwere partly destroyed during the war, but the production \nquickly resumed and the first aircraft equipped with \nturbojets (Caravelle de Sud-Aviation, Hawker-Siddeley \nTrident, Vickers VC10, BAC 1-11 of British Aircraft \nCorporation, etc.) emerged in the 1950s. The \ncompany, which is 100% -owned by t he industrial group \nof the same name, manufactures more than half of the \nairliners produced in the world and is Boeing\u0027s main \ncompetitor (Ville, 2006; Norris, 2010; Airbus).  \nAirbus was founded as a consortium by European \nmanufacturers in the late 1960s. Airbus Industry \nbecame a SAS (simplified joint-stock company) in \n2001, a subsidiary of EADS renamed Airbus Group in \n2014 and Airbus in 2017. BAE Systems 20% of \nAirbus between 2001 and 2006 (Gunston, 2010; \nLaming, 2000). In 2010, 62,751 people are employed \nat 18 Airbus sites in France, Germany, the United \nKingdom, Belgium (SABCA) and Spain. Even if parts \nof Airbus aircraft are essentially made in Europe some \ncome from all over the world. But the final assembly lines \nare in Toulouse (France), Hamburg (Germany), Seville \n(Spain), Tianjin (China) and Mobile (United States). Airbus \nsubsidiaries are also located in the United States, China, \nJapan and India (Airbus, From Wikipedia). \nAirbus produced its first aircraft, the A300, in 1972 \nand offers a range of commercial aircraft ranging from \nthe A318 to the A380, as well as aircraft and aircraft for \nbusiness men and women. Airbus was the first \nmanufacturer to install an electric flight control system on \nthe A320. The arrival of jet engines marks the beginning \nof the era of jet aircraft and the newer aircraft (DC-8, \nBoeing 707, Boeing 720) dominate the air market. In \nEurope, the infrastructures of the aeronautical industry \nwere partly destroyed during the war, but the production \nquickly resumed and the first aircraft equipped with \nturbojets (Caravelle de Sud-Aviation, Hawker-Siddeley \nTrident, Vickers VC10, BAC 1-11 of British Aircraft \nCorporation, etc.) emerged in the 1950s. They did not \nmeet the same success as their American competitors, \nsold much less and failed to penetrate the US market. \nIn the 1960s, mass air transport was booming and an \nFAA study forecast a tripling of traffic between 1965 \nand 1971 for a market of 1,610 aircraft. At the Paris Air \nShow in 1965, the main European airlines held informal \ndiscussions on their short- and mediumhaul needs, which \nwere necessary to respond to the growth in traffic. The \nAmerican manufacturers are engaged in the construction \nof wide-body aircraft (Lockheed L-1011, Boeing 747, \netc.), whereas in order to avoid frontal competition, \nEuropeans are interested in a different market, short sea \nhaul Two hundred places, more suited to the short but \ndense links encountered in Europe and seek to develop \nthe idea of \"airbuses\". \nMeetings between the main players in air transport take \nplace and European manufacturers all follow their own \nprojects: Galion for South Aviation, successor to BAC 1-11 \nfor British Aircraft Corporation, an extended version of the \nTrident for Hawker-Siddeley, Etc. The \ncompany, which is 100% -owned by t he industrial group \nof the same name, manufactures more than half of the \nairliners produced in the world and is Boeing\u0027s main \ncompetitor (Ville, 2006; Norris, 2010; Airbus).  \nAirbus was founded as a consortium by European \nmanufacturers in the late 1960s. Airbus Industry \nbecame a SAS (simplified joint-stock company) in \n2001, a subsidiary of EADS renamed Airbus Group in \n2014 and Airbus in 2017. BAE Systems 20% of \nAirbus between 2001 and 2006 (Gunston, 2010; \nLaming, 2000). In 2010, 62,751 people are employed \nat 18 Airbus sites in France, Germany, the United \nKingdom, Belgium (SABCA) and Spain. Even if parts \nof Airbus aircraft are essentially made in Europe some \ncome from all over the world. But the final assembly lines \nare in Toulouse (France), Hamburg (Germany), Seville \n(Spain), Tianjin (China) and Mobile (United States). Airbus \nsubsidiaries are also located in the United States, China, \nJapan and India (Airbus, From Wikipedia). \nAirbus produced its first aircraft, the A300, in 1972 \nand offers a range of commercial aircraft ranging from \nthe A318 to the A380, as well as aircraft and aircraft for \nbusiness men and women. Airbus was the first \nmanufacturer to install an electric flight control system on \nthe A320. The arrival of jet engines marks the beginning \nof the era of jet aircraft and the newer aircraft (DC-8, \nBoeing 707, Boeing 720) dominate the air market. In \nEurope, the infrastructures of the aeronautical industry \nwere partly destroyed during the war, but the production \nquickly resumed and the first aircraft equipped with \nturbojets (Caravelle de Sud-Aviation, Hawker-Siddeley \nTrident, Vickers VC10, BAC 1-11 of British Aircraft \nCorporation, etc.) emerged in the 1950s. They did not \nmeet the same success as their American competitors, \nsold much less and failed to penetrate the US market. \nIn the 1960s, mass air transport was booming and an \nFAA study forecast a tripling of traffic between 1965 \nand 1971 for a market of 1,610 aircraft. At the Paris Air \nShow in 1965, the main European airlines held informal \ndiscussions on their short- and mediumhaul needs, which \nwere necessary to respond to the growth in traffic. The \nAmerican manufacturers are engaged in the construction \nof wide-body aircraft (Lockheed L-1011, Boeing 747, \netc.), whereas in order to avoid frontal competition, \nEuropeans are interested in a different market, short sea \nhaul Two hundred places, more suited to the short but \ndense links encountered in Europe and seek to develop \nthe idea of \"airbuses\". \nMeetings between the main players in air transport take \nplace and European manufacturers all follow their own \nprojects: Galion for South Aviation, successor to BAC 1-11 \nfor British Aircraft Corporation, an extended version of the \nTrident for Hawker-Siddeley, Etc. The company, which is 100% -owned by the industrial \ngroup of the same name, manufactures more than half of the airliners \nproduced in the world and is Boeing\u0027s main competitor. Airbus was \nfounded as a consortium by European manufacturers in the late 1960s. \nAirbus Industry became a SAS (simplified joint-stock company) in 2001, a \nsubsidiary of EADS renamed Airbus Group in 2014 and Airbus in 2017. \nBAE Systems 20% of Airbus between 2001 and 2006. In 2010, 62,751 \npeople are employed at 18 Airbus sites in France, Germany, the United \nKingdom, Belgium (SABCA) and Spain. Even if parts of Airbus aircraft are \nessentially made in Europe some come from all over the world. But the final \nassembly lines are in Toulouse (France), Hamburg (Germany), Seville \n(Spain), Tianjin (China) and Mobile (United States). Airbus subsidiaries are \nalso located in the United States, China, Japan and India. Airbus produced its \nfirst aircraft, the A300, in 1972 and offers a range of commercial aircraft \nranging from the A318 to the A380, as well as aircraft and aircraft for business \nmen and women. Airbus was the first manufacturer to install an electric flight \ncontrol system on the A320. In 2013, Airbus produced 626 aircraft and won \n1,503 net orders. This is the best commercial result in the history of aeronautics. \nAt the beginning of 2017, Airbus announced that it had broken its own record \nof deliveries with the production of 688 aircraft this year, thus becoming No. 1.  \n \nKeywords: Aviation, Airbus Commercial Aircraft, Airbus, Airbus Group, \nAirbus Industry, European Aeronautics Manufacturer, The Flight, \nSpacecraft Propulsion, Jet Engines \n \nIntroduction \nAirbus Commercial aircraft, known as Airbus, is a \nEuropean aeronautics manufacturer with headquarters in \nBlagnac, in the suburbs of Toulouse, France. The \ncompany, which is 100% -owned by t he industrial group \nof the same name, manufactures more than half of the \nairliners produced in the world and is Boeing\u0027s main \ncompetitor (Ville, 2006; Norris, 2010; Airbus).  \nAirbus was founded as a consortium by European \nmanufacturers in the late 1960s. Airbus Industry \nbecame a SAS (simplified joint-stock company) in \n2001, a subsidiary of EADS renamed Airbus Group in \n2014 and Airbus in 2017. BAE Systems 20% of \nAirbus between 2001 and 2006 (Gunston, 2010; \nLaming, 2000). In 2010, 62,751 people are employed \nat 18 Airbus sites in France, Germany, the United \nKingdom, Belgium (SABCA) and Spain. Even if parts \nof Airbus aircraft are essentially made in Europe some \ncome from all over the world. {"@text":"1\nEuropean Industrial Policy:\nThe Airbus Case\nDamien Neven, University of Lausanne\nPaul Seabright, University of Cambridge\n1\n                                                \n \n   \n1\n This paper reports the results of a simulation study commissioned by the UK Department of\nTrade and Industry (EC/4878). Extracts from the Study are reproduced with the permission of\nthe DTI and the Controller of HMSO. We are grateful to the Air Division of DTI, and especially\nto Michael Hodson and Robert Waters, for their detailed help and advice; to John Sutton for\ncomments on the report of the original study; to David Begg and Gene Grossman for comments\non the first draft of this paper; to Lars-Hendrik Roeller for comments and advice throughout the\nproject; and to Lisa Anderson for outstanding research assistance. The usual disclaimer applies\nwith particular force: the views reported in the paper are those of the authors alone, and not\nthose of any of the above individuals or institutions.\n\n2\nAbstract\nThis paper estimates the impact that Airbus’s presence has had on the market for large\ncommercial airliners.  Our model reproduces (in a multi-stage) game a stylised characterisation\nof six main stages in the development of the large commercial airliner market, allowing for\nthree players (Boeing, Airbus and McDonnell Douglas) and four market segments.  The model\nis then used to ask a number of counterfactual questions about what would have happened in a\nvariety of circumstances (notably ones in which Airbus did not enter the market).  Besides\ncapacity and product developments, we also model the level of expenditures on research an\ndevelopment in order to see whether Airbus’s presence has had an impact on the type and\ntechnological specification of aircrafts produced.  We find that given the prior presence of\nMcDonnell Douglas in this market, Airbus has had only a modest impact on the prices of\ncommercial airlines (an average of 3.5%).  The reasons are twofold : first, although the Airbus\npresence constraints the actions of Boeing, it weakens the incentive for McDonnell Douglas to\ncompete vigorously with Boeing.  Secondly, by reducing Boeing’s market share, it prevents the\nrealisation of the substantial economies of scale and scope that are believed to exist in this\ntechnology.  Overall, this means that the consumer surplus argument for government subsidy to\nAirbus is only weakly supported by the model.  Consumer surplus benefits from a challenge to\nBoeing have certainly been substantial but most of them could have been achieved by\nMcDonnell Douglas on its own.  In terms of product development, we find that although\nAirbus may have deterred McDonnell Douglas from producing an aircraft in the same category\nof the A 300 (medium range, medium-bodied), it may in contrast have actually made it easier\n\n3\nfor McDonnell Douglas to produce the MD-11 in competition with the A 330/340 and the\nBoeing 777.  This is because the loss of scale and scope economies by Boeing as a result of the\nAirbus entry has substantially raised the cost to Boeing of producing the 777, making entry\nmore attractive for McDonnell Douglas even when Airbus’s presence is taken into account. \nFinally, we find that the presence of Airbus reduces Boeing’s profits by at least $ 100 bn and\nMcDonnell Douglas’s by two-thirds.  Airbus itself makes profits which are difficult to estimate\nwith confidence, but which may lie somewhere between $49bn and $52bn, of the order of a\nbillion dollars per annum and equivalent to a rate of return over the whole period of between\n6% and 11%.   If we give the same weight to profits and consumer surplus, this implies that\nAirbus has had a large negative impact on world welfare but a comfortably positive impact on\nEuropean welfare.\n\n4\n  \n1. Introduction\nWhen should governments intervene to promote specific types of productive activity in\nthe economy? Answers to this question have been subject to periodic swings of fashion, but a\nconsensus has gradually emerged that intervention needs to be based on a sound account of\nwhy unaided markets will fail to encourage adequately efficient levels of the activities\nconcerned, as well as a reasonable optimism that government failures will not lead to\ndistortions as significant as those market failures it is sought to correct. The application of this\nconsensus to actual cases, however, has generated substantial discord, particularly when the\nactivities under discussion are not public goods, but private goods which for one reason or\nanother are claimed to be supplied in inadequate quantity or quality. That the state should be a\nvigilant referee of the competitive process is a view that would command widespread assent;\nthat it should be an active player in the competitive game is a much more debated and\ndebatable claim.\nIn no specific field of economic activity has the debate been more vigorous than in\ncommercial aerospace, where production has been supported and encouraged in covert or overt\nways by friendly governments around the world. Many reasons can be imagined for the\nfavoured status of aerospace, from the cynical (\"politicians like shiny toys\") to those more\nfirmly grounded in an analysis of market failure. There are persuasive grounds for thinking that\naerospace is likely to be subject to market failures, notably because of large scale economies in\n\n5\nproduction and the importance of research and development. Furthermore, these market\nfailures are often difficult for individual countries to overcome on their own, so aerospace has\ngiven rise to significant international co-operation, the success or failure of which has\nsometimes been seen as an important indicator of the prospects for co-operation in other fields.\nThe most celebrated instance of such cooperation is the European Airbus consortium,\nwhich was formed in the late 1960s to challenge the dominance of the Boeing Corporation in\nworld markets; in 1994 for the first time, the former sold more commercial aircraft than the\nlatter. Its rivalry with Boeing and McDonnell-Douglas (MDD, also of the United States) has\nled to fierce claims, in the GATT and other fora, about the role of public funding in generating\n\"unfair\" competition. \nThe question what benefits flow from government support for commercial aerospace is\nparticularly pertinent to Airbus because the consortium owes its very existence to explicit\ndecisions by collaborating governments. Broadly speaking, three kinds of benefit have been\nthought to flow from the Airbus presence in the market for large commercial jet airframes. The\nfirst consists of lower prices to consumers resulting from a challenge to a dominant producer\n(Boeing), benefits that could not be supposed to motivate a purely commercial competitor. The\nsecond consists in various kinds of economic spillover from the advanced technology\nembodied in the Airbus models; these might consist in the adaptability of technological\nadvances to other {"@text":"Review\nAdventures in Semantic Publishing: Exemplar Semantic\nEnhancements of a Research Article\nDavid Shotton*, Katie Portwin, Graham Klyne, Alistair Miles\nImage Bioinformatics Research Group, Department of Zoology, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom\nAbstract:Scientific innovation depends on finding,\nintegrating, and re-using the products of previous\nresearch. Here we explore how recent developments in\nWeb technology, particularly those related to the\npublication of data and metadata, might assist that\nprocess by providing semantic enhancements to journal\narticles within the mainstream process of scholarly journal\npublishing. We exemplify this by describing semantic\nenhancements we have made to a recent biomedical\nresearch article taken fromPLoS Neglected Tropical\nDiseases, providing enrichment to its content and\nincreased access to datasets within it. These semantic\nenhancements include provision of live DOIs and hyper-\nlinks; semantic markup of textual terms, with links to\nrelevant third-party information resources; interactive\nfigures; a re-orderable reference list; a document summary\ncontaining a study summary, a tag cloud, and a citation\nanalysis; and two novel types of semantic enrichment: the\nfirst, a Supporting Claims Tooltip to permit ‘‘Citations in\nContext’’, and the second, Tag Trees that bring together\nsemantically related terms. In addition, we have published\ndownloadable spreadsheets containing data from within\ntables and figures, have enriched these with provenance\ninformation, and have demonstrated various types of data\nfusion (mashups) with results from other research articles\nand with Google Maps. We have also published machine-\nreadable RDF metadata both about the article and about\nthe references it cites, for which we developed a Citation\nTyping Ontology, CiTO (http://purl.org/net/cito/). The\nenhanced article, which is available at http://dx.doi.org/\n10.1371/journal.pntd.0000228.x001, presents a compel-\nling existence proof of the possibilities of semantic\npublication. We hope the showcase of examples and\nideas it contains, described in this paper, will excite the\nimaginations of researchers and publishers, stimulating\nthem to explore the possibilities of semantic publishing\nfor their own research articles, and thereby break down\npresent barriers to the discovery and re-use of information\nwithin traditional modes of scholarly communication.\nIntroduction\nOnline versions of journal articles are conventionally presented\neither as HTML Web pages or as static PDF documents, with the\nWeb used primarily as a convenient distribution medium for\ntraditional text. As the electronic embodiment of the printed page,\nthe PDF document is both familiar and easy for humans to read,\nbut it is antithetical to the spirit of the Web, lacking user\ninteractivity and being difficult for machines to read, thus\ninhibiting the development of services that can automatically link\ninformation between articles.\nRecent developments in Web technology can be used for\nsemantic enhancement of scholarly journals articles, providing\nbetter linking to other resources, adding descriptive metadata that\nassist article discovery and specify the meaning of concepts and\nterms within the article, and allowing users access to ‘‘lively’’\ncontent in the form of interactive figures, re-orderable reference\nlists, document summaries, and downloadable numerical datasets\nin which the data are both accessible and actionable.\nIn this paper we describe semantic enhancements made to a\nrecently published biomedical research article from the journal\nPLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases(PLoS NTDs), using this single\nexemplar research article to create a compelling proof of the\npossibilities of semantic publication.\nWe define the termsemantic publicationto include anything that\nenhances the meaning of a published journal article, facilitates its\nautomated discovery, enables its linking to semantically related\narticles, provides access to data within the article in actionable\nform, or facilitates integration of data between articles.\nWe undertook this exercise in semantic publishing to demon-\nstrate some of the different types of semantic enhancement that we\nconsider desirable for improving the usefulness of online research\narticles, and to show the benefits that ensue from publishing the\ndata they contain to the Web, thus facilitating the integration of\ninformation from different publications.\nThe Unique Role of the Journal Article\nSince our contention is that biomedical journal articles should\nbecome better {"@text":"Towards a Semantic Search Engine\nfor Scientiﬁc Articles\nBastien Latard\n1,2(B)\n, Jonathan Weber\n1\n, Germain Forestier\n1\n,\nand Michel Hassenforder\n1\n1\nMIPS, University of Haute-Alsace, Mulhouse, France\nbastien.latrad@uha.fr\n2\nMDPI AG, Basel, Switzerland\nAbstract.Because of the data deluge in scientiﬁc publication, ﬁnding\nrelevant information is getting harder and harder for researchers and read-\ners. Building an enhanced scientiﬁc search engine by taking semantic rela-\ntions into account poses a great challenge. As a starting point, semantic\nrelations between keywords from scientiﬁc articles could be extracted in\norder to classify articles. This might help later in the process of browsing\nand searching for content in a meaningful scientiﬁc way. Indeed, by con-\nnecting keywords, the context of the article can be extracted. This paper\naims to provide ideas to build such a smart search engine and describes\nthe initial contributions towards achieving such an ambitious goal.\n1 Introduction\nKeeping up-to-date in a speciﬁc research ﬁeld is a tedious and complex task. This\nis mandatory as it allows researchers to increase their knowledge on a domain and\nacquire latest ideas. Hence, choosing the correct approach is the ﬁrst step of any\nresearch work. Despite—or because of—the data deluge in scientiﬁc publication,\nresearchers spend a signiﬁcant amount of time searching for articles related to\ntheir scientiﬁc interests.\nAn editorial fromNature[1] clearly expressed the continued frustration of\nthe scientiﬁc community concerning the incredible potential that text mining\nof scientiﬁc literature represents. However, text miners often face the barrier of\npublishers’ legal restrictions (i.e., closed access). The average growth of scien-\ntiﬁc literature is estimated to be 3 million new articles per year from journals\nand conferences over the last 4 years, with 3.3 million articles produced in 2016\n(http://www.scilit.net). This massive amount of data is published by more than\n6000 publishers in around 47,000 scientiﬁc journals. These de-centralised and\nseparated platforms further complicate the research process because scientists\nare unable to go through them all in order to search for relevant articles. Thus,\nthey have to rely on big databases or indexing companies which provide either\nan incomplete corpus due to selection criteria or only display articles from their\nown platforms. Moreover, their search engines often oﬀer very limited search\nfunctionalities, and this is the problem we want to tackle.\ncﬀSpringer International Publishing AG 2017\nJ. Kamps et al. (Eds.): TPDL 2017, LNCS 10450, pp. 608–611, 2017.\nDOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-67008-9\n54\n\nTowards a Semantic Search Engine for Scientiﬁc Articles 609\nTo tackle this problem, our approach consists in using semantic relations\nbetween keywords to extract the main categories of the articles. This approach\nsimultaneously validates both the context of the article and the context of the\nword, thus providing the correct category. Eﬀendy and Yap [2] discussed the\npotential of using semantic mining tools to extract the best category of a con-\nference. This is exactly what our framework aims to do.\n2Method\nOur approach uses BabelNet [3] which is a multilingual lexicographic and ency-\nclopaedic database based on the smart superposition of semantic lexicons (Word-\nNet, VerbNet) together with other collaborative databases (Wikipedia and other\nWiki data). A query for a term through BabelNet returns “dictionary entries”,\nsynonyms, categories or domains. Each synsetScontains the relative categories\nC, domainsDand synonymssynwithin the speciﬁc concept:\nS\u003d{C, D, syn}\t(1)\nAssuming that synonyms of keywords might be an interesting way to connect\nseveral articles, BabelNet is the knowledge database on which our framework will\nrely. However, BabelNet lacks speciﬁcity and searching for one word can return\nsynsets from various diﬀerent contexts. For example, “ﬂight” returns 36 synsets,\nfrom a South Korean movie to the verb ‘to ﬂy’. Consequently, a method to ﬁlter\nout unrelated synsets is mandatory.\nBecause synonyms are too speciﬁc, and domains are too general, categories\nhave been naturally chosen in order to identify overlapping between synsets from\ndiﬀerent keywords. Indeed, if several keywords share the same category, then this\nis potentially the correct category in regards to the article context. In addition,\nthe greater the number of keywords sharing the same category, the higher the\nconﬁdence. Thus, connecting the returned synsets based on their categories is\nan interesting way to naturally ﬁlter out all of the unrelated synsets.\nThis approach does ﬁlter some content, but still returns “living people;\nEnglish-language ﬁlms; celestial mechanics; American ﬁlms” as the main cat-\negories for keywords “nonlocal gravity; celestial mechanics; dark matter”.
